title: Consensus
concept: Consensus is how a group of replicas agree on one value, or one order of values, even though machines crash and messages are lost or delayed. The usual answer is a majority: a cluster of 2f+1 nodes elects a leader, the leader appends each change to a replicated log, and a change counts as committed once a majority has stored it. Because any two majorities overlap, the system can lose a minority of nodes and still agree, which is what lets a strongly consistent system stay available as long as a quorum survives. The cost is a round trip to that majority on every write, so consensus trades latency for agreement.

points: Consensus is how a group of replicas agree on one value, or one order of values, even though machines crash and messages are lost.
A leader appends each change to a replicated log, and a change counts as committed once a majority has stored it.
Any two majorities overlap, so a minority of nodes can fail and the system still agrees; the cost is a majority round trip on every write.
The etcd guide says commit latency has a floor set by the network round trip between members plus a durable disk write.

prerequisiteReasons.cap: Consensus takes from CAP the choice of strong consistency, and the cost that the system keeps serving only while a quorum of nodes survives.
prerequisiteReasons.replication: Consensus takes from replication the picture of several copies of the same data, which must all apply the same changes in the same order.

why.outcome: After this you can explain what problem consensus solves and why a majority is the key idea.
why.body:
Replication gives you several copies of the data, and CAP tells you that during a partition you must choose between answering and being correct. Consensus is the machinery that lets you choose correct while staying available for as long as possible: it lets a set of replicas agree on exactly one history of changes, so every surviving replica tells the same story.

The trick is the majority. In a cluster of 2f+1 nodes, a decision only counts once more than half have recorded it. Any two majorities share at least one node, so a later decision always overlaps an earlier one through that shared witness, and the group can never agree to two conflicting histories. This also means the cluster keeps working while up to f nodes are down or cut off, because the remaining majority can still decide. Lose the majority, though, and the system stops rather than risk disagreeing with itself.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture a leader, a replicated log, and a majority commit.
mentalModel.body:
Think of one leader and a set of followers, each holding an identical append-only log of commands. A client sends a command to the leader. The leader appends it to its log and sends it to the followers. Once a majority (including the leader) has written it durably, the leader marks it committed and tells the client, and the followers apply it in the same order.

Two things keep this safe. First, there is only ever one leader for a given term: a node becomes leader only by winning votes from a majority, and two different majorities cannot both exist, so there cannot be two leaders making decisions at once. Second, a follower only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so a new leader can never be missing a committed entry. If the leader dies, its followers notice the missing heartbeats, and after a randomised timeout one of them stands for election and, with a majority of votes, becomes the new leader.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through leader election, log replication, commit by majority, and what happens when the leader fails.

steps.step: Size the cluster for the failures you must survive
steps.explanation: To tolerate f failures you need 2f+1 nodes: three to survive one, five to survive two. The odd size means a majority always exists and two majorities always overlap.

Time is divided into terms. A node that misses the leader's heartbeats times out, becomes a candidate, and asks for votes. A node grants its vote only to a candidate whose log is at least as current as its own; a candidate with a majority of votes becomes leader.

steps.step: Replicate the log from the leader
steps.explanation: Clients send commands only to the leader. The leader appends each to its log and sends it to followers to append in the same position, keeping every log identical in order.
An entry is committed once the leader has stored it on a majority of nodes. Only then does the leader apply it and answer the client, so a committed entry is on enough nodes to survive f failures.

A naive read must also confirm leadership with a majority, which is slow. Systems often give the leader a time-bounded lease so it can answer reads locally while the lease holds, avoiding a round trip per read.

If the leader crashes or is partitioned away, its followers stop hearing heartbeats and, after a randomised timeout, one stands for election. Because a new leader needs a majority and an up-to-date log, no committed entry is ever lost.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace a write and a leader failure through a three-node cluster and see why nothing committed is lost.

steps.explanation: Nodes A (leader), B and C each hold the same log. The cluster tolerates one failure, because a majority is two of three.

A client sends "set x = 5" to A. A appends it and sends it to B and C. B stores it and acknowledges; now A and B, a majority, hold it, so A commits it and answers the client, even before C catches up.
A crashes. B and C stop hearing heartbeats. After a randomised timeout, B becomes a candidate and asks C for a vote.
C compares logs: B's log includes "set x = 5" and is at least as current as C's, so C votes for B. B now has two votes, a majority, and becomes leader for a new term.
Because B had the committed entry and only an up-to-date node could win, "set x = 5" is still there. A client reading from the new leader sees x = 5. No acknowledged write was lost.

If both A and C were down, B alone is not a majority, so it cannot commit new writes or even safely serve them. The cluster blocks rather than risk disagreeing, which is the availability price of staying correct.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid the three most common mistakes in reasoning about consensus.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: Why do consensus clusters use an odd number of nodes like 3 or 5?
options: Because odd numbers are faster to replicate to
So every node can be a leader at once
So a majority always exists and any two majorities overlap, preventing two conflicting decisions
quiz.why: A cluster of 2f+1 has a clear majority, and because any two majorities share a node, the group can never commit two conflicting histories.
wrong: Replication speed does not depend on whether the node count is odd or even. The odd count helps because it forms a non-ambiguous majority.
There is at most one leader per term; multiple simultaneous leaders is exactly what consensus prevents.

quiz.question: When is a log entry considered committed in a leader-based consensus system?
options: As soon as the leader writes it to its own log
Once a majority of nodes have stored it durably
Only after every single node has stored it
quiz.why: A majority storing the entry means it will survive up to f failures and that any future leader must have it, so the leader can safely apply and acknowledge it.
wrong: The leader alone is not enough; if it then crashed, the entry might be lost or unknown to the next leader.
Requiring all nodes would make the system unavailable whenever any node is down, which defeats fault tolerance.

quiz.question: A five-node cluster has two nodes down. Can it still commit writes?
options: Yes, the remaining three are a majority, which is enough to commit
No, a five-node cluster tolerates only one failure, so with two nodes down every write must stop
Only reads can continue, because a write needs every node to be up and acknowledging it
quiz.why: Five nodes tolerate two failures because three still form a majority; the cluster keeps committing until it loses the majority.
wrong: A cluster of five tolerates two failures because three still form a majority.
Both reads and writes can proceed while a majority survives; requiring every node would defeat fault tolerance.

quiz.question: The leader crashes just after committing an entry on itself and one follower. Why is that entry safe?
options: A new leader must win a majority and have an up-to-date log, so it already holds the entry
The crashed leader will come back and replay it, because a leader's log is always kept on disk
Entries are never really lost, because every client keeps a cached copy and resends it if needed
quiz.why: Only a node whose log is at least as current as a majority can win the election, and the entry is on a majority, so the winner has it.
wrong: Safety cannot depend on the crashed node returning; it may never come back.
The client cache is not the system of record; durability comes from the majority holding the entry.

quiz.question: What is the main cost a consensus system pays for its guarantees?
options: It can never tolerate any node failure, because every node must acknowledge every write
It must store the data on only one node, to avoid ever having to coordinate replicas
A write needs a round trip to a majority, which adds latency
quiz.why: Every committed write waits for a majority to acknowledge, so network and disk round trips to those nodes set a latency floor.
wrong: Tolerating failures is what consensus is for, so it is a benefit rather than a cost.
Consensus replicates to many nodes, not one; single-node storage would not be fault tolerant.

quiz.question: Why do production systems often give the leader a time-bounded lease?
options: To allow two leaders at once, so both halves of a partitioned cluster keep accepting writes
So the leader can serve reads locally without a majority round trip while the lease holds
To remove the need for any leader, since the lease lets every node accept writes by itself
quiz.why: A lease lets the leader know it is still the leader for a bounded time, so reads are safe to answer locally, avoiding a coordination round trip on every read.
wrong: Two concurrent leaders would break safety; a lease is designed to guarantee the opposite.
A lease is a property of the leader, not a way to eliminate the leader role.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe what limits consensus performance in a real system and one way production databases make it cheaper at scale.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can tell apart the physical latency limits of consensus and the engineering that reduces its overhead.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can size a cluster, reason about reads under leases, and plan consensus across regions.

exercises.prompt: A team runs a 2-node consensus cluster "to save money" and is surprised it cannot tolerate a single failure. Explain what went wrong and fix it.
exercises.answer: Two nodes have no clear majority: a majority of 2 is 2, so losing either node leaves one node that cannot form a majority and the cluster blocks. Consensus needs 2f+1 nodes to tolerate f failures, so use three nodes to survive one. Three nodes still only commit when two agree, but now one can be down and the other two still make progress.
exercises.tradeoffs: Three nodes cost more than two but are the minimum that tolerates a failure. Adding more (five) tolerates two failures at the price of a larger majority to wait for on every write.
wrongAnswers: Add a second leader so either node can decide alone.
Keep two nodes but let a lone node commit, which risks split-brain disagreement.
Use an even number like four, which tolerates the same one failure as three but needs a larger majority.

exercises.prompt: Reads on your consensus-backed store are slow because each one confirms leadership with a majority. Design a way to serve reads quickly without risking stale or wrong answers.
exercises.answer: Give the leader a time-bounded lease: while the lease is valid the leader knows no other leader can exist, so it can answer reads from its local state without a majority round trip. Renew the lease before it expires, and run health checks so a failed leaseholder is detected and a new one is chosen. Tie the lease to the consensus leadership so the two cannot disagree, as CockroachDB's leader leases do.
exercises.tradeoffs: Leases add renewal traffic and the machinery to detect a dead leaseholder; at scale that renewal cost itself must be managed. A lease also bounds how quickly a new leader can safely take over, since the old lease must be known to have expired.
wrongAnswers: Serve reads from any follower with no freshness check, risking stale data.
Drop to a weaker consistency without telling callers.
Keep paying a majority round trip on every read and just add hardware.

exercises.prompt: You need a consensus cluster spanning three regions on different continents. Writes feel slow. What is the floor on write latency, and what do you do about it?
exercises.answer: Each committed write needs a majority to acknowledge, so if the majority spans continents the write pays at least one cross-region round trip, which can be tens to hundreds of milliseconds. You cannot beat the speed of light, so you reduce how often you pay it: place the majority of replicas (and the leader) in the region that does most of the writing, keep a minority elsewhere for survival, and batch requests into each consensus round. If different data is written from different regions, run separate consensus groups per shard, each with its leader near its writers.
exercises.tradeoffs: Concentrating the majority in one region makes writes from there fast but writes from far regions slower, and losing that region is more impactful. Per-shard groups localise latency but add many consensus groups to operate.
wrongAnswers: Assume a global cluster can have single-digit-millisecond writes everywhere.
Put all replicas in one region, losing cross-region fault tolerance.
Lower the quorum below a majority to go faster, breaking safety.

next.outcome: After this you can choose the next topic that builds on consensus.
next.body: Consensus is the engine under Distributed transactions, where shards must agree to commit together. It also underpins Failover, which is leader election by another name, and it is how a CAP-consistent system keeps a single agreed history while a quorum survives. Replication is the layer consensus coordinates.

posts.title: etcd Performance
posts.ageNote: This is versioned documentation (v3.5), not a dated post. The page shows "Last modified June 14, 2021", a line tied to a change in the documentation's repository, so it is shown as a last-modified date and not as a publication year. Its benchmark table was run on etcd 3.2.0, so treat those numbers as old. It is here for what it says limits consensus commit latency: the network round trip between members and the disk sync, which are physical limits rather than release details.

digest.problem: The guide explains what defines etcd's performance, latency and throughput, and why commit latency is limited by two physical constraints, so a reader can see what a consensus system costs before sizing or placing a cluster.
digest.constraints: etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to replicate requests among members and reach agreement. The guide says commit latency is limited by network IO latency and disk IO latency: the minimum time to finish a request is the round trip between members plus the time fdatasync needs to commit data to permanent storage.

walkthrough.step: Define performance as latency and throughput
walkthrough.explanation: The guide frames two numbers: latency, the time to complete one operation, and throughput, the operations completed per second. It notes that average latency tends to rise as throughput rises under concurrent load.
Requests are replicated among members and agreed through the Raft consensus algorithm, so each request pays for communication between members and for writing to disk.

The minimum time to finish a request includes the network round trip between members. The guide gives a typical round trip of about 50 ms within the United States and as slow as 400 ms between continents, and says a round trip within a datacenter can be several hundred microseconds.
Each member must persist the entry. A typical fdatasync on a spinning disk is about 10 ms, while on an SSD it is often under 1 ms, so disk choice directly shapes commit latency.
To get high throughput despite these per-operation costs, etcd batches multiple requests together and submits them to Raft as a group, amortising the round trip and the sync over many entries.

numbers.value: ~50 ms US, up to 400 ms intercontinental
numbers.meaning: Typical network round-trip time between members, the first limit on consensus commit latency
Typical fdatasync (durable disk write) latency, the second limit; for SSDs the guide says it is often under 1 ms
What a three-member cluster can complete under heavy load in common cloud environments; under light load it finishes a request in under 1 ms

tradeoffs.chosen: Raft consensus to replicate requests among members, with batching: etcd groups multiple requests and submits them to Raft together so it keeps high throughput under heavy load.
tradeoffs.why: The guide says commit latency is limited by network and disk latency, so the minimum time for a request is one round trip plus one fdatasync. It says batching is what lets etcd reach high throughput despite heavy load. It names no alternative design that was considered.

digest.failures: The guide gives no failure account: it describes no incident, mistake or abandoned approach. It does state limits. The minimum request time is one round trip between members plus one fdatasync. A typical round trip is about 50 ms within the United States and as slow as 400 ms between continents, and a spinning disk's fdatasync is about 10 ms. Average latency usually rises as throughput rises under concurrent requests. Snapshots can double observed latency on a spinning disk, and gRPC adds latency, especially for local reads.
digest.takeaways: Consensus latency has a floor set by the network round trip between members plus a durable disk write, so you make it faster by shrinking those, with nearby members and SSDs, and by batching requests into Raft. Knowing the two limits is what lets you place and size a consensus cluster sensibly.

posts.edition: page shows last modified June 14, 2021, v3.5 documentation

digest.problem: CockroachDB splits data into many Ranges, each replicated and kept consistent by Raft. To serve reads quickly without coordinating with the other replicas on every request, each Range designates one replica, the leaseholder, as the authoritative source. But every leaseholder must continually renew its lease and be health-checked, and as a cluster grows to hundreds of thousands or millions of Ranges, that constant renewal traffic becomes a substantial CPU cost.
digest.constraints: Each Range needs one replica holding a lease to serve reads without coordinating on every request, and a large cluster has hundreds of thousands or even millions of Ranges. The two earlier lease types each fail one way: expiration leases cost a Raft write per renewal, and centralized leases depend on a single Range.

walkthrough.step: Use a leaseholder for fast reads
walkthrough.explanation: Within each Range, one replica holds a lease making it the authoritative source, so reads can be served from it without a round trip to the other replicas on every request.

walkthrough.step: See the renewal cost at scale
walkthrough.explanation: A leaseholder holds a temporary lease it must periodically renew, and the system health-checks leaseholders to detect failures. Across hundreds of thousands or millions of Ranges, the renewal traffic adds up to a substantial CPU cost.

walkthrough.step: Tie the lease to Raft leadership
walkthrough.explanation: Leader Leases integrate lease ownership tightly with Raft leadership, so the replica that is the Raft leader is the one that holds the lease, rather than tracking the two separately.

Leader Leases combine decentralized health checks with that tighter Raft integration, aiming for the low cost of centralized leases without a single point of failure, and the reliability of expiration leases without the CPU overhead of constant renewals.

The post says the safety properties of the Liveness Fabric are formally verified in TLA+, and that Leader Fortification prevents a leader from losing leadership unexpectedly, so the leaseholder can always be the Raft leader. It also reports recovery within seconds from node crashes, network partitions and disk stalls.

numbers.meaning: Reduction in lease-maintenance CPU usage at scale from Leader Leases, the post's headline result
Ranges in a large cluster, each previously renewing its own lease, which is why the renewal CPU added up
Each Range designates one of its replicas, the leaseholder, as the authoritative source of truth that serves reads without coordinating on every request

tradeoffs.chosen: Tie lease ownership to Raft leadership and use decentralized health checks, so the leaseholder's fast local reads are kept without a separate stream of lease-renewal messages.
tradeoffs.rejected: Centralized leases (a single point of failure) and plain expiration leases renewed constantly (reliable but CPU-heavy at scale).
tradeoffs.why: The post says expiration leases cost CPU through constant renewals and centralized leases concentrate a critical dependency in one Range. Leader Leases are presented as the low cost of centralized leases without the single point of failure, and the reliability of expiration leases without the renewal overhead.

digest.failures: The post gives no failure account of Leader Leases: it announces a paper and describes no incident or abandoned design of its own. It does state limits of the two earlier lease types. Expiration-based leases are reliable, but each renewal is a Raft write, so the cost adds up across hundreds of thousands or even millions of Ranges. Centralized leases are much cheaper, but if the one Range holding every node's health status becomes slow or unavailable, every centralized lease is affected.
digest.takeaways: Consensus in production includes how a leader proves it is still the leader so it can serve reads. Merging the leader and leaseholder roles into one replica, and moving health checks to the node level, removed a per-Range overhead that only showed at scale; the post reports up to 85% less lease-maintenance CPU in its experiments.

comparison:
Both posts are about leader-based consensus at scale, but one explains its unavoidable costs and the other removes an avoidable one, so they read well together as the floor and then the optimisation. etcd's performance guide is the fundamentals: why a Raft commit costs a network round trip between members plus a durable disk sync, with figures for each. CockroachDB's leader-leases post is the engineering on top: how to keep the fast-read benefit of a leader without paying a separate stream of lease-renewal messages for every one of millions of Ranges.

Where they diverge is which cost they target. etcd's limits are physical, the speed of the network and the disk, and the guide's advice is to shrink them (SSDs, nearby members) and batch, not to eliminate the round trip. CockroachDB's cost is one the software created for itself, lease renewal traffic, and the fix is architectural: fold lease ownership into Raft leadership and decentralise health checks so the renewals go away. One post says "here is the floor you cannot beat"; the other says "here is overhead above the floor that you can."

The evidence matches that split. etcd gives the physical numbers, a round-trip time of about 50 ms within the US and up to 400 ms between continents, and a disk sync of about 10 ms on a spinning disk versus under 1 ms on an SSD. CockroachDB gives an engineering result, lease-maintenance CPU cut by up to 85% at scale across hundreds of thousands or millions of Ranges. Together they show consensus performance is part physics you must plan around and part overhead you can design away, as long as you keep the one-authoritative-leader guarantee intact.

glossary.definition: Getting a group of replicas to agree on one value or one order of values despite crashes and lost messages.
More than half the nodes; a decision counts once a majority records it, and any two majorities overlap.
The cluster size needed to tolerate f failures: three survive one, five survive two.
The single node, per term, that accepts client commands and replicates them to followers.
The ordered, append-only sequence of commands every replica stores identically.
A period with at most one leader; a new election starts a new term.
The process where a node times out, becomes a candidate, and wins a majority of votes to lead.
Marking a log entry durable and applicable once a majority has stored it.
A widely used consensus algorithm designed for understandability, with a leader and replicated log.
A time-bounded grant letting the leader serve reads locally without a majority round trip while it holds.
In CockroachDB, the replica of a Range that holds the lease and serves its reads authoritatively.

mistakes: Running an even number of nodes, especially two, and expecting fault tolerance. A majority of two is two, so losing either stops progress; you need 2f+1 (three to survive one, five to survive two).

Thinking the leader can answer reads from local state for free. Without a lease, a safe read must confirm leadership with a majority; a stale former leader could otherwise serve old data after a partition.

Assuming consensus can be fast across continents. Every commit needs a majority round trip, so a globe-spanning quorum pays cross-region latency on every write; you place the majority near the writers rather than wishing the round trip away.
